scenarios.context: Two friends in their twenties discuss why it is so hard to buy a home.

speakerA.en: House prices in this city have risen so fast that saving for a deposit seems almost impossible. How is anyone supposed to cope?
Would rent controls help? At least renters would know what to expect.
So what's the alternative? Surely we can't just wait for prices to fall.
People don't want construction on their doorstep, and I can partly understand that.
What about a tax on empty properties? There are thousands of flats nobody lives in.
I'd support that. It seems a fairer approach than forcing young people to leave the city.

speakerB.en: It's a structural problem. Wages have grown slowly, while prices have been pushed up by limited supply and investors buying second homes.
In the short term, yes. But economists warn that landlords may stop maintaining their properties, or leave the market altogether.
Building more homes is the most effective long-term solution, though that means overcoming local opposition to new developments.
So can I, but it's a classic case of individual interest clashing with the common good. Had cities built more in the past, we wouldn't be in this situation.
That would make owners think twice about leaving them vacant, and it wouldn't cost the public anything.
Agreed. Without a combination of measures, the gap between homeowners and everyone else will only widen.

scenarios.scenario: Flexibility or security in the gig economy
scenarios.context: A delivery rider and a university student discuss working through an app.

speakerA.en: You work for a delivery app, don't you? I've always wondered whether the flexibility is as good as it sounds.
No sick pay or holiday pay, I assume?
That seems unfair. Shouldn't the company be responsible for protecting its workers?
Is there a middle way? Perhaps a minimum hourly rate plus basic insurance.
But wouldn't higher costs lead to higher prices for customers?
I'd certainly do so. It's easy to forget that a cheap delivery depends on someone's unstable job.

speakerB.en: In some ways it is. I choose my hours, so I can fit work around lectures. The downside is that nothing is guaranteed.
Exactly. Officially I'm self-employed, so if I fall ill or have an accident, I lose my income immediately.
Many riders think so, and there have been court cases about it. The companies argue that treating us as employees would destroy the flexibility.
That would be a big improvement. Some countries have introduced a third category of worker with limited rights, which seems a sensible compromise.
Probably, though many customers say they'd pay a little more if they knew workers were treated fairly.
That's all I ask: that people think about the person behind the app.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues debate whether the richest citizens should pay higher taxes.

speakerA.en: A recent report shows that the richest one per cent now own more than the bottom half of the population combined. Isn't that unacceptable?
Some governments have introduced exit taxes to prevent exactly that. Surely the real issue is political will.
The evidence on that is mixed. Many countries with high taxes still have thriving economies and stronger public services.
Fair enough. Yet inequality isn't only a moral problem; it can weaken social trust and even slow growth.
Opportunity matters, but how can children from poorer families compete if their schools are underfunded?
So we agree on more than we thought.

speakerB.en: It's certainly worrying, but I'm not sure higher taxes are the answer. Wealthy people can move their money abroad.
Perhaps. But high taxes may also discourage investment and entrepreneurship, which create jobs for everyone.
That's true, although they also have strong institutions and low corruption. Not every country can say the same.
I accept that. Where we disagree is on the method. I'd focus on education and opportunity rather than redistribution.
A strong point, and it shows that the two approaches aren't mutually exclusive. Taxes could pay for better schools.
It seems so. The disagreement is about balance, not about the goal.

scenarios.context: A grandfather and his granddaughter discuss the future of pensions.

speakerA.en: Grandad, my economics teacher says there will soon be too few workers to pay for everyone's pension. Is that really true?
So will my generation ever receive a pension at all?
That doesn't seem fair. You paid in for forty years and retired at sixty.
What could be done now? Raise the retirement age?
I'd rather save while I'm young, but my salary barely covers my rent.
So the solution has to involve everyone, not just individuals.

speakerB.en: There's some truth in it. People live longer and have fewer children, so each worker supports more retirees than in my day.
I expect so, but probably at an older age and on less generous terms than I enjoyed.
I did, and I'm aware of how lucky I was. Had governments reformed the system earlier, the changes today would be less painful.
That's one option, but it's hard on people in physically demanding jobs. Encouraging immigration and private savings could help too.
I know, and that's the dilemma of your generation. Should wages continue to stagnate, saving for old age will become even harder.
Exactly. A pension system is a promise between generations, and it only works if both sides keep it.

scenarios.context: Two students argue about giving every citizen a guaranteed monthly income.

speakerA.en: Some people propose a universal basic income, a fixed monthly payment to every citizen. Do you think it could ever work?
Supporters say it would replace many existing benefits, which would reduce administration costs.
Fair. What about the argument that it would make people lazy?
That surprises me. I expected a bigger drop in employment.
Then why hasn't any country adopted it permanently?
Were the trials to run for longer, perhaps the evidence would persuade them.

speakerB.en: It's an attractive idea, but I'd want to know how it would be funded. Giving everyone money is extremely expensive.
That's possible, but some people would lose out if their current support were worth more than the flat payment.
The pilot projects I've read about don't support that. Most recipients kept working, and some used the security to retrain or start businesses.
So did many economists. Stability seems to give people the confidence to take sensible risks rather than to give up.
Mostly because of cost and politics. Voters are sceptical of anything that sounds like free money for everybody.
Possibly. Until then, I think a targeted version for the most vulnerable groups may be more realistic.
